LONDON OP IN I )N. "PAM§ is France" the Parisians say, and they may be right although that is doubtful. London is Great Britain, the Londoners say, and they are wrong without any doubt. But it is impossible to fathom the depth of: Metropolitan conceit. We do not mean the conceit of the common vulgar cockney but of much higher classes of people—society, as it is called, clubmen. and writers in news- papers. These people believe that they form and guide the opinion of the country, the real fact being that out of London they have little or no influence, and even in the metropolis their influence reaches only an inconsiderable portion of the population. Take the newspaper writers for instance No doubt the pnnopal daily papers such as the Times, Daily Newt, Telsyraph, Standard, are extensively read in the country, and have their due effect upon opinion, but such papers as the Pall Hall Gaulle, the Saturday Het ww, the Globe, and the Hominy Poet, are to the great Maso of the people "fountains shut up and books sealed." it is we believe a fact that only 17 copies of the Pall Mall Gaulte come into Manchester. The other large towns in the provinces are not likely to take a larger proportionate number, and yet this pretenti .us and conceited journal write, as if it were a power in the State instead of being only the means of affording an hours daily reading toloungem at the clubs, and to people going from the city Is their homes after business. Even as regards the journals which we have men- tioned as exceptiona to the general obscurity, the larger country towns have papers of their own just as good, as well informed, se well written, and much more largely circu- lated. There is no writer in the TIM/ equal In ability to the chief leader writer in the Manchester Demeter. In general sagacity, knowledge of affairs, and sound political I judgment, no one who knows the two men would prefer Mr Delano to Mr. Dunakley. The way in which the London journals speak of country affairs is moreover extra. , ' ordinary in its dogmatism and ignoranee. At the end of the Salford election, for instance, the Daily New, told us that the I Liberals were defeated because Mr. May weed to vote for Mr. Butt's motion. Tie writer of that artide probably knew ! nothing of eford, and very, likely I was never in Lancashire in his , life. We knew perfectly well that his , theory was absurd. Nobody °minuted with I tlts Salford election ever heard a complaint of Mr. Kay on the ground alleged by the writer in the Daily News. It is certain that the electors of Salford would have been as much surprised if Mr. May had refused to support Mr, Butt's resolution as they would . have been thirty years ago if any Libera, had refused to vote;for Mr. Cobden's motion for a seleot committee to enquire into the effect of the Corn Laws upon agriculture The information which the Metropolitao journals profess to give us upon general affairs is often equally untrustworthy and ridicilous. Not long ago • leading writer in Truth told us that a mutiny of troops in India had been prevented by a large distri- bution of money by the British Government amongst the discontented soldiers. It is difficult to conceive of a writer upon the staff of any paper who could give currency if; • report on absurd, and it in difficult to conceive zff the manager of any paper hav- ing a writer so ffbeurd upon his staff. Ii was the World, we be:lfge, that told us a short time since that Mr. Glacis:ne had all his life relied upon somebody to lead and guide him in his political career. At present we were told, Mr. Chamberlain was his minter, and he was entirely in the leading strings of the junior member for Birming. ham, It is not easy to imagine a more ludicrous idea than that of a veteran states- man like Mr. Gladstone, eepecially • rim so self-willed and self-reliant as he is, taking instructions from a young politician who has only just completed his first full I session in Parliament. obese are only instances of the ridiculous mistakes—to put it mildly—of the London press, especially the most pretentious, and 60 far as tit, provinces are concerned, the most obscure portion ef The London correspondents of the country I press again are equally dogmatic and unre- liable. Many of them no doubt are men of ' extensive general knowledge, and of great literary ability; but many of them are of quiteanother type. They criticise men whose , &co latchet they are not worthy to unloose, and of measures of which they cannot but be I profoundly ignorant, with the most confident assurance. We know some specimens of this order, and judging according to our knowledge we should, may that a man of this class gets acquainted with the waiters of the Carlton and the entree to the lobbies of the Houle. lie has the power of writing a cer- tain slip-shod English, and under the signs- ture " Mor N," as the catechism haa it, he ! sends down special information to the country which we ignorant provincials ;are i expected to swallow as serious truth. The fact is, that he is only the retailer of gossip —tiny worse, of adulterated gossip—the . crumbs and droppings of conversation at club-tables gathered. from " demos's," who repeat the conversation of men only very little leas ignorant than themselves. It is not our intention to disparage the use- ' fulnese and influence of the press generally. c„'jit have a proper contempt for the bird that fouls it ozn neat. We stand by our order. I But we have no _aispoeition to encourage pretenders that have no .sober 1,84,)° than self-conceit. We even venture to :--nk that we are magnifying our office as a part on the provincial press in protesting against the I assumptions of some of the London journals. We believe we are doing some good by ridiculing "London Assurance" generally. No good can arise from allowing any section of the community to think more highly of itself than it ought to think. " Society " may have its uses, its advantages, its rights, but the" upper ten thousand " are not the people of Great Britain and Ireland. Their journals tell us that they are "written by gentlemen for gentlemen," but with all their "gentility" they are blind guides. As for Osman Pasha, who was to do so much, he appears to be in danger , of losing his supplies by being cut off from Sophia and thus being obliged to cal itulate or to fight his way through the Russian forces entrenched before him. 'blue, the defeat of the Russians at Plevna, though of undeniable gravity, has not had the ruinous result which many persons expected. The Turks have been unable to gain any other advantages since the battle took place, and their opportunity of obtaining any, diminishes daily with the arrival of Russian reinforcements, which continue to arrive in masses. It is intimated that in less than a month the Russian army will be reinforced by the addition of 100,000 men, including 50,000 guards, when there will be in the field more than 300,000 Russian soldiere. It may be assumed that this cut host will not be brought merely to wait oaths defensive ; a much smaller army would be sufficient to guard the Russian positions, as is tacitly acknowledged by the Turks. What is meant by the concentration of many troops in Bulgaria is doubtless that the Russians intend shortly to strike a decisive blow pre- paratory to their march to Adrianople, an achievment, however, that is looked upon by , some military nettles as gigh,ly improbable. this year, but which the Russiape must surely hope to accomplish seeing that they are straining every nerve and putting forth every effort in their power. If the Czar had given up all hope of securing victory this year, where would be the necessity of hurry- ing to the front the finest troops in the Em- pire. It cannel be that 300,000 Russians are required to defend t eir positrons against half that number of Turks, or that the Czar in- tends so great • force to remain in Bulgaria during the winter. This we may look upon I as impossible ; for Bulgaria, devesta ed as it has been, can afford nothing like the sup- plies that will be neoeasary for so large an army, and if this winter is similar to last, it will not be possible to bring supplies across the Danube. Their successful advance if it takes plea will be viewed by some people with alarm, by others with satisfaction, and by all with anxiety. Those who consider the success of Russia to be opposed to the interests of the British Empire, and whose prejudioe have blinded them to the true character of Turk- ish rule, will be filled with dismay at the sight of Russian victories, whilst there who have noted the corruption and barbarity which seem inseparable from Ottoman dominion, will rejoice over the likelihood of the Christian problem, of Turkey being freed from the abominable yoke under which they have so long groaned. Yet no one can look forward to tke establishment of the supremacy of Russia over Turkey without anxiety. With the experience we have had of the Turkish sympathies of some of our ministers, es- pecially of Lord Beammatield, who does not disguise his sympathies for the Ottoman power, the announcement of Russian chum- ram will be the cause of alarm. It will not a ,on be forgotten that notwithstanding the professions of neuirelity which the . nglish Government have made, the English fleet , wee despatched to ries.ka Bay, and a number 'of troops hurried to Malta, immediately I after the woman" had crossed the Balkans. Happily the English nation has declared in emphatta tones that Turkey has forfeited for ever the support of this oountry, and although there is a noisy minority, beaked by a portion of the preset, that would like ' above all things to see an English alliance formed with Turkey against Russia, iii. tolerably certain that the majority of the people, whose sympathies are net Turkish, will defeat so unrighteous a project if it is ever attempted. Mr. Gladstone last week pointed out the necessity of vigilance, and his advise ought to be taken to heart by everyone who fear" to see English aid given to the Cause of oppression and cruelty. Parliameat is now dispersed, and its members are scattered all over Europe; the policy of the country will therefore be for the next six months largely in the hands of ministers who have shown their pro-Turkish sympathies over and over again, and if they are to be prevented from hindering the liberation of the oppressed subjects of Tur- key, the people of England will have to maintain an unceasing watchfulness, and be prepared to take immediate action whenever there is a sign of the 'lightest deviation from the policy of neutrality which the Government has pledged itself to maintain.
